title: Agentix: An Efficient Serving Engine for LLM Agents as General Programs
type: peer-reviewed conference paper / official open-access page
evidence: The paper treats agentic programs as dynamic workflows of LLM calls and external interrupts. It reports call-level and program-level head-of-line blocking, and reports 4–15x program-throughput improvement at the same latency versus vLLM in its evaluated workloads.
relevance: Confirms that program-level context matters; rules out presenting a generic LLM-call scheduler as new. Its scheduler primarily schedules LLM calls; tool-resource ownership, cancellation and durable recovery remain outside the central evaluated mechanism.

title: JITServe: SLO-aware LLM Serving with Imprecise Request Information
type: peer-reviewed conference paper / official open-access page
evidence: The abstract identifies latency-sensitive, deadline-sensitive and compound requests with evolving dependencies; it reports 1.4–6.3x service-goodput improvement or 28.5–83.2% resource savings across chat, deep-research and agentic workloads. The paper notes workload shifts and prediction errors as limitations.
relevance: Shows that end-to-end SLOs are a current service problem, not just GPU utilization. A course project should use deadline/SLO metrics, but should not claim to invent SLO-aware LLM scheduling.

title: Llumnix: Dynamic Scheduling for Large Language Model Serving
type: peer-reviewed conference paper / official open-access page
evidence: The paper describes heterogeneous and unpredictable request resource/latency requirements, severe queueing delays, poor tail latency and SLO violations; it uses runtime rescheduling and live migration across model instances.
relevance: Established baseline for dynamic LLM request scheduling. Any proposed project must distinguish itself from GPU/model-instance rescheduling.

title: Parrot: Efficient Serving of LLM-based Applications with Semantic Variable
type: peer-reviewed conference paper / official open-access page
evidence: LLM applications/agents may contain complex workflows with multiple LLM requests. The paper argues that request-level public APIs hide application-level relationships and can produce suboptimal end-to-end performance.
relevance: Confirms that application/workflow context is necessary. A project cannot claim that simply adding workflow metadata is a new contribution.

title: Orla: A Library for Serving LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
evidence: Orla separates stage mapping, workflow orchestration and memory management; workflows combine multiple LLM steps, tool calls and heterogeneous infrastructure. The abstract reports latency/cost improvements from stage mapping and lower time-to-first-token from workflow-level cache management.
relevance: Shows that workflow orchestration and tool-aware stages are already an active systems direction. It is a strong related work, not evidence that the space is empty.

title: Architectural Implications of Agentic AI Workflows
venue: arXiv preprint; production-scale Microsoft Azure characterization reported
evidence: The study characterizes agentic workflows as fragmented, heterogeneous sequences of LLM inference, tool invocation and orchestration that cross CPU–GPU boundaries. It reports CPU critical-path pressure, bursty/imbalanced load, stranded CPU/GPU capacity and locality/coordination costs; the Agora prototype uses role-aware CPU affinity and adaptive resource reclamation.
relevance: Directly validates the OS-level resource problem. It also means a project should not claim that CPU/GPU role-aware scheduling is unexplored; the feasible gap is a smaller tool-resource and failure-aware runtime on commodity OS resources.

title: Agentic Coding in the Wild: Characterizing GitHub Copilot Traces at Production Scale
evidence: The abstract reports 3.2M users, 13M sessions, 761M LLM calls and 95T tokens in sampled June 2026 traces. Coding-agent turns interleave LLM calls and tool execution; token use, session duration and tool calls are long-tailed. The paper reports average within-turn KV-cache hit rate of 90%, falling to 55% across turn boundaries. Its full paper reports that around 9% of turns can trigger retry-driven compute amplification up to 4x, and that mutation/command tools have long-tailed runtimes and lower success rates than read/search tools.
relevance: Provides concrete production pain beyond abstract LLM serving: tool execution is frequent, heterogeneous, failure-prone and responsible for tail latency. The authors explicitly list quality-aware scheduling and server-side resource metrics as limitations/future work.

title: SAGA: Workflow-Atomic Scheduling for AI Agent Inference on GPU Clusters
authors: Dongxin Guo, Jikun Wu, Siu Ming Yiu
evidence: SAGA treats a full agent workflow as a scheduling unit, reports 1.64x lower task completion time, 1.22x GPU memory utilization and 99.2% SLO attainment on SWE-bench/WebArena workloads, but also reports about 30% lower peak throughput than throughput-optimal batching.
relevance: Strong counter-evidence: workflow-level scheduling is already being actively solved at the GPU-cluster level. It motivates selecting host-side tool contention/failure recovery rather than reproducing GPU scheduling.

title: Fairness in Serving Large Language Models
type: peer-reviewed conference paper / official open-access page
evidence: The paper argues that request-rate limits are a crude fairness mechanism because request lengths differ; it defines token-cost-aware service fairness and proposes VTC for continuous batching.
relevance: Useful fairness baseline. Do not use token fairness alone as the project novelty.

title: Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve
type: peer-reviewed conference paper / official open-access page
evidence: The paper identifies prefill/decode interference and reports higher serving capacity under tail-latency constraints using chunked prefills and stall-free schedules.
relevance: Establishes that low latency versus throughput is a solved-but-still-active serving tradeoff at the inference-engine layer; this should be a baseline, not the whole project.

title: ExoFlow: A Universal Workflow System for Exactly-Once DAGs
type: peer-reviewed conference paper / official open-access page
evidence: ExoFlow separates execution from recovery and lets workflow tasks specify execution semantics, addressing the runtime/recovery-overhead tradeoff for heterogeneous pipelines.
relevance: Supports durable task state and checkpoint/recovery as legitimate system concerns, but exactly-once workflow systems are established; the course project should use a scoped at-least-once/idempotent model.

title: A survey on LLM-based multi-agent systems: workflow, infrastructure, and challenges
evidence: The survey organizes LLM multi-agent systems around profile, perception, self-action, interaction and evolution, and discusses infrastructure and current challenges.
relevance: Useful overview source; not evidence for a specific performance gap by itself.

title: OSWorld: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Open-Ended Tasks in Real Computer Environments
evidence: OSWorld evaluates 369 real computer tasks across web/desktop apps and reports a large gap between human and agent success in its evaluation. It makes tool use and OS file I/O part of the benchmark workload.
relevance: Supports realistic tool-workflow evaluation, but task success is not the same as serving performance; use it only to motivate workload construction.
